entities.summary:
Giacomo Gastaldi (died 1566) emerged as a preeminent Italian cartographer, astronomer, and engineer in 16th-century Venice, a pivotal figure who significantly advanced the empirical understanding of global geography during the Age of Exploration. His work profoundly challenged and gradually superseded the long-dominant Ptolemaic worldview, providing Europe with some of its most accurate and widely disseminated maps of the newly discovered and explored regions. Operating from the bustling commercial and intellectual hub of the Republic of Venice, Gastaldi was at the forefront of a cartographic revolution driven by new navigational data and printing technologies, directly influencing how Europeans conceived of the world.

His most celebrated contributions include the detailed regional maps for Giovanni Battista Ramusio's monumental three-volume travelogue, *Delle Navigationi et Viaggi* (1550–1559), which documented global explorations and was a cornerstone of Renaissance geographical knowledge. Gastaldi also produced groundbreaking single-sheet world maps, such as *La Universale Descrittione del Mondo* (1546) and *Il Disegno della Geografia Moderna* (1561), which were among the first to depict the Americas with increasing accuracy and to feature a more precise representation of Asia. His innovative use of copperplate engraving allowed for finer detail and greater dissemination, moving away from older woodcut traditions and incorporating the latest Portuguese and Spanish expeditionary data.
